verses.1:
Al-Mizan takes idhā to forecast a future divine help and victory, consoling the Prophet and furnishing one of the Qur’an’s glad tidings and foretellings. It rejects both the reading that makes the terms cover every instance of aid to him—including his battles and the conversions of the Anṣār and Yemen—and the reading that identifies the victory with Ḥudaybiyyah: neither accords with people entering the religion in throngs. The clearest reading is the conquest of Mecca, the greatest victory of his life and the divine collapse of Arabian polytheism. The promised “mighty help” in (48:1-3), revealed at Ḥudaybiyyah, most likely foretold support against Quraysh and the conquest two years later; this is more fitting than the peaceful conversion of Yemen. The sūrah therefore falls after the treaty and Sūrah al-Fatḥ but before the conquest.

Al-Mizan explains afwāj as rapidly moving groups, so the verse means that people would enter Islam group after group; “Allah’s religion” is Islam, as in (3:19). The victory has two correlated sides: polytheism and falsehood are defeated, while monotheism and truth are raised. Tasbīḥ fits declaring God free of imperfection; taḥmīd fits praise for the blessing. The commands to glorify, praise, and seek forgiveness also make the servant remember God’s majesty and beauty and his own weakness and dependence after the Prophet’s strenuous work of uprooting falsehood has been eased, thereby completing gratitude. Since the Prophet is already forgiven—his intrinsic deficiencies already covered—his seeking forgiveness asks for the continuing, not initial, divine covering; God’s being All-Relenter both explains and urges that request.

Al-Mizan records differently worded narrations that read the sūrah as announcing the Prophet’s death: ʿAbbās wept when he heard it, understood that meaning, and the Prophet confirmed it; the author explains this by the completion of his mission and the principle that decline follows an apex. Umm Salamah reports that near the end of his life he continually said subḥān Allāh wa bi-ḥamdihi, astaghfiru Allāh wa atūbu ilayhi, explaining that he had been commanded to do so by this sūrah; the author notes further reports with variant wording. Imam al-Ṣādiq is reported to call “Read, in the name of your Lord” the first revealed sūrah and Sūrah al-Naṣr the last; the author suggests this may mean the last revealed in its entirety.

A lengthy narration links the conquest to Quraysh’s breach of the Ḥudaybiyyah arrangement: Khuzāʿah had allied with the Prophet and Banū Bakr with Quraysh; after Quraysh armed and secretly aided Banū Bakr against Khuzāʿah, ʿAmr b. Sālim appealed to the Prophet. The Prophet vowed to aid Banū Kaʿb, while Quraysh’s later attempt through Abū Sufyān to renew the treaty found no effective support. The account says that the Prophet ordered preparations while asking God to keep the plan from Quraysh, and that Ḥāṭib’s warning letter was intercepted through revelation. In Ramadan of 8 AH he set out with ten thousand Muslims and about four hundred horsemen. It further recounts ʿAbbās securing Abū Sufyān’s safety, his eventual profession of faith, and his viewing the Muslim force; when he called the Prophet’s power a kingdom, ʿAbbās corrected him that it was prophethood.

The same report says Abū Sufyān, Ḥakīm, and Budayl were sent to summon Quraysh to Islam, with safety promised to those in Abū Sufyān’s or Ḥakīm’s house, or in their own closed homes. Al-Zubayr was placed at Mecca’s high point, Saʿd led an Anṣār vanguard, and Khālid entered from below; weapons were to remain sheathed except against attackers, though four men and two women were excepted and named for execution. When Saʿd’s cry suggested massacre and captivity, the Prophet had ʿAlī take his flag and enter gently. At the Kaʿbah, the narration has the Prophet proclaim God’s fulfillment of His promise, cancel claims of property, privilege, and blood except custody of the Kaʿbah and supplying pilgrims with water, reaffirm Mecca’s inviolability, and release Quraysh as al-ṭulaqāʾ. It explains their mass conversion by the fact that their lives had been placed in his hands without fighting, making them fayʾ. It also reports Ibn al-Zibaʿrī’s conversion and verse of repentance.

Ibn Masʿūd reports that at the conquest the Prophet struck the 360 idols around the Sacred House while reciting (34:49) and (17:81). Ibn ʿAbbās reports that he would not enter while idols remained; after images of Abraham and Ishmael holding al-azlām were removed, he denounced the idolaters for knowing that the two had never used them. Al-Mizan says that many narrations concern the conquest, that this account is itself only a summary, and directs readers seeking more to hadith collections and Prophetic sīrah.
